verified_how: Public pricing page, public API reference and public docs, fetched 2026-08-18. NO API key was used and nothing was synthesised (#247 forbids it).

supersedes.why: That file is a DOM dump of elevenlabs.io/pricing with a `url:` and a `fetched: ... (200)` header and NO DATE anywhere in it, so it cannot be aged. Re-checked against the live page on 2026-08-18: every tier name, price and credit figure still matches, so the snapshot has not drifted. It carries one trap, recorded below as `creator.price_trap`.

notes: Prices in USD. `credits_per_month` is the subscription allowance. A credit is NOT always a character — see `credit_per_character`, which is the single most load-bearing correction in this file.

tiers.commercial_note: VERBATIM from docs/help-center/legal: "The free plan does not include a commercial license and cannot be used for any commercial purpose." Publishing from Free additionally requires attributing elevenlabs.io in the title. **This makes Free unusable for any narration that ships in Foray**, which removes the obvious "pilot it for nothing" option. A pilot must start at Starter.

Lowest tier that grants commercial use. "All paid plans include a commercial license, provided you're not using Beta Services." Beta Services output may not be used commercially or in production at ANY tier.

tiers.price_trap: The pricing card renders as "$22 First month 50% off / $11per month", and a scrape reads that as $11/month. It is not. The FAQ on the same page disambiguates: "Creator $22 (121,000 credits, $11 for the first month)". **$11 is a first-month promotion, not a standing price.** The #247 cost sketch described the target as "their $6-11/month tiers"; in that band there is exactly ONE standing tier, Starter at $6.

credit_per_character.ui_note: VERBATIM, and repeated identically on every model's help-center page: "For UI generations, 1 character costs 1 credit, excluding credit multipliers. API generations are discounted." So the discount below is API-ONLY. A cost model that assumes a cheap model halves the burn in the web app is wrong.
credit_per_character.api_note: The only OFFICIALLY BOUNDED statement is the pricing FAQ's "costing between 0.5 and 1 credit per character" for Flash/Turbo API usage. The 0.5 endpoint is STRONGLY IMPLIED — docs/models says Flash v2.5 is "50% lower price per character for API generations", and elevenlabs.io/pricing/api lists Flash/Turbo at $0.05 per 1K characters against Multilingual v2 at $0.10, a clean 2x — but NO primary page publishes a numeric per-model credit multiplier. Treat 0.5 as strongly-implied-but-uncited and budget at 1.0 unless a real run measures otherwise.
credit_per_character.voice_multiplier_warning: The phrase "excluding credit multipliers" points at a SECOND multiplier axis: Voice Library community voices carry an owner-set multiplier that STACKS on the model rate. The docs confirm the mechanism; no primary page publishes the values. **A voice chosen from the community library can therefore cost more per character than the model rate implies** — a reason to prefer a first-party/default voice, or to measure before committing. This is a live unknown, not a solved input.

api_dollar_per_1k_chars.source: elevenlabs.io/pricing/api, which quotes dollars per 1K characters and mentions no credits at all.

overage.consumption_order: subscription credits first, then PAYG balance
overage.usd_per_1000_credits_note: NOT PUBLISHED, and deliberately so: "PAYG pricing varies depending on whether you're generating content using the API or the UI." Legacy usage-based billing quotes a fixed per-1,000-credit price that is "displayed when you enable usage based billing", i.e. only visible inside an account. Third-party blogs circulate $0.30/$0.24/$0.18/$0.12 per 1K for Creator/Pro/Scale/Business; the primary source (help.elevenlabs.io) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so those numbers are UNVERIFIED and are not recorded as fact here.
overage.public_marginal_proxy_note: The pricing compare table's "Extra minutes" row — verified live, and the best PRIMARY public proxy for marginal cost. Per minute, not per 1,000 credits.

rollover.requires: an active paid subscription with no downgrade or cancellation
rollover.forfeit_note: Downgrading or cancelling forfeits unused credits at the end of the cycle. PAYG top-ups sit outside the rollover cap but expire 12 months after purchase.
rollover.why_it_matters_here: Narration generation is BURSTY — a Foray is authored and then voiced in one go. Rollover to 3x quota means a tier can absorb a burst up to three times its monthly number, which changes the tier answer for a one-time corpus build.

output_formats.default_note: VERBATIM from docs/api-reference/text-to-speech/convert. 128 kbps mp3 needs NO upgrade — it is the API default and the pricing compare table lists "128 kbps, 44.1kHz" for Free, Starter and Creator alike.

tier_gated.mp3_44100_192: Creator or above per the API reference; the pricing page instead advertises 192 kbps as a Pro-and-above upgrade. **The docs and the marketing page disagree and this was not resolvable from public sources.** Assume Pro if 192 kbps ever matters.

output_formats.recommended_why: Narration is one dry mono voice, which 64 kbps carries cleanly, and it quarters the bytes against the 128 kbps default (see docs/narrator-pipeline.md for the hosting arithmetic). Going lower is tempting and should be resisted: narration sits directly against publisher tape at every seam, and an audible quality drop at the join is the exact artefact the 2.0 s seam beat exists to smooth over. 32 kbps saves 6 MB a Foray and spends it on sounding like a different, worse product.

provider_implied_rate.derivation: The pricing page's own minutes column: 10,000 credits is quoted as ~10 minutes and 121,000 as ~121 minutes. Exactly 1,000 credits per minute in both.
provider_implied_rate.why_it_matters: This is the PROVIDER'S OWN characters-to-minutes conversion, and at 1 credit per character it means 1,000 characters per minute of speech. That is 19% ABOVE the 840 chars/min used in the #247 sketch and 14% above the 880 this repo measured. Since characters are what get billed, a LOW chars/min rate UNDERSTATES the cost of a fixed duration budget. It is probably a round marketing number rather than a measurement, but it is the provider's, it errs toward the expensive side, and it is therefore the right figure to BUDGET with.
